rationale: Tests ability to identify circumcorneal congestion as a danger sign distinguishing anterior uveitis/acute glaucoma from benign conjunctivitis — a classic OP trap (Khurana ch. Uveitis).
A classic OP trap: patients with acute angle-closure glaucoma can present with nausea/vomiting, misleading the clinician toward a GI diagnosis and delaying eye treatment (Khurana).
Tests understanding of the papillary vs follicular reaction — the single most important clinical sign for differentiating bacterial from viral conjunctivitis (Khurana/Parsons').
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) management trap — topical steroids are contraindicated in most viral conjunctivitis but may be used cautiously only in specific EKC complications (Parsons').
Tests WHO SAFE strategy knowledge — a high-yield OP topic for exams and the basis of India's National Trachoma Control Programme (Khurana).
Tests the critical distinction that trachoma causes blindness via corneal scarring (pannus + entropion/trichiasis), NOT directly via optic nerve or retinal disease.
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) causes a corneal shield ulcer — a high-yield clinical sign unique to VKC that students frequently confuse with infectious corneal ulcer (Khurana/Parsons').
Tests understanding that mast cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglicate, olopatadine) must be used prophylactically BEFORE allergen exposure — a common counselling error (Khurana).
The probe test to distinguish pterygium from pseudopterygium is a classic clinical viva question (Khurana) — pseudopterygium is not adherent at the limbus.
Tests understanding that recurrence rate is the main surgical concern with pterygium and that conjunctival autograft significantly reduces recurrence versus bare sclera excision (Khurana).
High-priority safety rule — never apply pressure if penetrating FB is suspected; this is a hard stop in OP skills training (Khurana/Parsons').
Subtarsal FB is the most commonly missed FB site — eversion of the upper lid is mandatory in all cases of FB sensation (Khurana).
Tests the fundamental pharmacokinetic fact that the conjunctival sac holds only 7-10 μL but a commercial drop delivers ~50 μL — most drug is wasted via overflow and nasolacrimal drainage (Khurana).
Multiple topical drops require a 5-minute interval — a commonly violated rule that reduces efficacy of both drugs (Khurana/clinical pharmacology).
